data.title: Illegal metal detecting damages our history
data.excerpt: Every year metal detectorists rob their own country of thousands of archaeological finds: they sell them to dealers abroad, keep them at home where no one can study them, or simply ruin them. Under § 249(1) of the Criminal Code, searching for archaeological finds with a metal detector is a criminal offence carrying one to five years in prison.
data.metaTitle: Illegal metal detecting damages our history
data.metaDescription: Illegal metal detectorists deprive the country of thousands of archaeological finds every year, sell them abroad and block professional research.

mediaTexts.alt: A prohibition sign with a crossed-out figure of a searcher with a metal detector

children.text: Every year metal detectorists rob their own country and its citizens of THOUSANDS of archaeological finds, which they:
sell on internet sites, above all to dealers abroad
store at home in an unprofessional way out of selfish motives, and so prevent their professional study, documentation and presentation to the public
ruin, if they have no financial or other value for them
-the find itself is not as important to an archaeologist as the context in which it lies; by looting we deprive ourselves of important information and insights
-every year metal detectorists destroy hundreds of find spots, making work and research at the archaeological site impossible and thereby destroying the history of the area concerned
-it may be in your own village or its surroundings that these thieves of history loot finds which, under other circumstances, would have made your village or town famous

blocks.alt: Illegal metal detecting damages our history

children.text: -finds that have lain hidden in the ground for thousands of years are best off under the ground, and they will last there until the arrival of an archaeologist, who knows best how to handle them, study them and publish them
-every find should be handed over to an archaeologist, or to an archaeological institution

Under § 249, paragraph 1 of the Criminal Code, searching for archaeological finds with a metal detector, as well as possessing archaeological finds, is a criminal offence carrying a prison sentence of 1 to 5 years.
